sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Tsukuyomi** ​(*tsukuyomi*) ‌— Moon ‌God, ​Shintō ​— belongs ​to ​the ​Japanese ‌tradition. The ​name ​means ‌"Moon reader"[^1].

​Tsukuyomi ‌is ​the ‌moon god, ​one ​of ​the three ​great ​heavenly ‌children ​born from ‌Izanagi's ​purification.

‌PuniCodex restores ​the ‌name ​as ‌**Tsukuyomi**. The ​plain ​ASCII ‌form *tsukuyomi* ‌is ‌the ​modern ​Hepburn romanization; ‌the ​restoration ​capitalizes the ‌conventional ​spelling. ​Because ‌the Japanese ​source ‌script ​uses ​logographic characters ​whose ​distinctive ‌visual form ‌cannot ​be ‌conveyed ​in the ​basic ‌Latin ‌alphabet, and ‌because ‌no ​diacritic ‌or special ​letter ​is ​added in ‌this ​restoration, ​the ​name is ‌placed ​in ​Tier 2. ​The ‌Unicode ​form ‌remains the ​philologically ‌complete ​reference, while ‌the ‌ASCII ​spelling ​is a ​practical ​convenience ‌for the ‌domain-name ​system[^2].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Japanese ‌characters as ​**月読**. Etymologically ​it means ​"Moon reader"[^1].

Tsukuyomi ​means "moon-reading" ​or "moon-counting," ‌from *tsuki* ​(moon) and ​*yomi* (reading/counting). ‌The name ​may refer to ‌the counting ​of months ‌or to ​the reading ​of the ​moon's phases. He ​is one ​of the ‌three great ​heavenly children ‌born from ​Izanagi's purification, together ‌with Amaterasu ​and Susanō.

‌The ASCII ​form *tsukuyomi* ‌survives only ​because the early ​domain-name system ‌could not ‌carry Japanese ‌characters or ​diacritics; it ​is a ‌technological compromise, not ​an ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Tsukuyomi** gives ​the conventional ‌Hepburn romanization with ​initial capitalization, ‌the standard ​scholarly way ​to cite ​a proper ​name in romanized ‌Japanese. The ‌name is ​Tier 2 ‌because the ​restoration does ​not add ‌a distinctive diacritic ‌or special ‌letter absent ‌from the ​ASCII form.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ​**t** → ​**T** — ‌Same
- ​**s** → ​**s** — ​Same
- **u** ‌→ **u** ​— Same
​- **k** ​→ **k** ‌— Same
​- **u** → ‌**u** — ​Same
- ‌**y** → ​**y** — ‌Same
- ‌**o** → ​**o** — Same
​- **m** ​→ **m** ​— Same
‌- **i** ‌→ **i** ​— Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The conventional ​reading of ‌the name ‌is **/tsɯ.kɯ.jo.mi/** ​— Modern ​Japanese (Standard ​Japanese)[^1].

For ​the modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'TSUKUYOMI' — ​pronounce each ‌vowel clearly ​and avoid ‌English diphthongs. Japanese ​is mora-timed, ‌so each ​syllable receives ​roughly equal ​weight.



Tsukuyomi ​is Tier 2 ​because the ‌ASCII form ​*tsukuyomi* already ‌represents the ​same phonemic ‌sequence; no ​stress mark, length ‌mark, or ​distinctive letter ‌is required ​to recover ​the spoken ‌name.

Japanese ‌is a mora-timed ‌language: each ​short syllable ​receives roughly ‌equal temporal ​weight, and ​long vowels ‌or double consonants ​count as ​separate morae. ‌The name ​**Tsukuyomi** therefore ‌falls into ​a regular rhythmic ​pattern that ​is lost ​if an ‌English speaker ‌stresses one ​syllable heavily[^2]. ‌The Hepburn romanization ​used here ​records the ‌modern standard ‌pronunciation; it ‌does not ‌preserve the ​historical pitch accent ‌of the ​word, which ​differs across ​dialects. When ‌reading the ​name aloud, ​keep the vowels ​pure and ‌avoid English ​diphthongs: the ​restoration **Tsukuyomi** ​is the ‌conventional scholarly citation ​form, not ‌a phonetic ​transcription with ‌added diacritics. ​Because the ‌ASCII string ‌*tsukuyomi* already encodes ​the same ​phonemic sequence, ​the name ​remains Tier ‌2 in ‌the PuniCodex ​system.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Tsukuyomi ​is the ‌moon god, ‌counterpart ​to his ​sister ​Amaterasu, the ​sun. His ​domain ‌is the ​night, ​the calendar, ‌and the ​measurement ‌of time. ​Unlike ‌the sun, ​which is ​associated ​with the ​imperial ​house, the ‌moon in ​Shinto ‌has a ​more ‌ambiguous and ​sometimes malevolent ‌role.

​The domain ‌of ​**Tsukuyomi** is ​understood within ‌the ‌broader Japanese ‌religious ​landscape as ​both a ‌specific ​functional sphere ​and ‌a node ​in a ​network ‌of kami, ​buddhas, ‌and local ​spirits. Shrines, ​temples, ​and household ​rites ‌all invoke ‌the figure ​in ‌ways that ​blur ​strict boundaries ‌between Shinto ‌and ‌Buddhist practice[^3]. ‌The ​restoration **Tsukuyomi** ‌therefore names ​not ​only a ​mythic ‌person but ​a living ​field ​of ritual ‌activity: ​pilgrimage, festival, ​iconography, and ​prayer ‌continue to ​define ‌what the ​name means ‌in ​contemporary Japan. ‌This ‌combinatory or ​"syncretic" context ​is ​essential for ​interpreting ‌the domains ‌listed above.
​

sources.citation: Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​*Kojiki* states ‌that Tsukuyomi ‌was born ​from ​Izanagi's right ​eye when ​he ​purified himself ‌after returning ​from Yomi. ​In ‌the *Nihon ​Shoki* he ‌kills the ​food ‌goddess Ukemochi ​in disgust ​at ​her method ​of producing ​food, causing ‌Amaterasu ​to separate ‌from him ​and refuse ‌to ​share the ‌sky. This ​is ‌why the ​sun and ​moon never ‌appear ‌together.

The ‌narrative of ​**Tsukuyomi** participates ​in ‌the larger ​mythic program ​of ‌the *Kojiki* ​and *Nihon ​Shoki*: to ‌explain ​the origins ‌of the ​imperial house, ​the ​division of ​divine labour, ‌and ‌the relationship ​between the ‌human and ​kami ​worlds. Because ‌these chronicles ‌were compiled ‌in ‌the eighth ​century under ‌imperial ​patronage, the ​myths also ​serve a ‌political ​theology, grounding ​earthly authority ​in divine ‌descent ​and cosmic ​order[^3]. Read ​comparatively, ‌the story ​of tsukuyomi ‌illustrates how ​Japanese ‌myth uses ​genealogy, descent ‌from heaven, ‌and ​the negotiation ​of rival ​domains ​to construct ‌a coherent ‌sacred history.
​

sections.label: Kojiki & Nihon Shoki
sections.body:
The ​*Kojiki* and ‌*Nihon Shoki* ‌are the ​earliest ​written witnesses ​to **Tsukuyomi**, ​although the ​figure ‌may have ​circulated in ​oral and ‌local ​cult forms ‌long before ​the eighth ‌century. ​In the ​chronicles, Tsukuyomi ​appears as ​the ​lunar kami ‌born when ​Izanagi washed ‌his ​right eye, ‌later separated ​from the ‌sun ​goddess Amaterasu, ‌embedded in ​the imperial ​genealogy ‌and the ‌narrative of ‌cosmic order[^1]. ​The ​*Kojiki* account ‌tends to ​privilege the ​mythic ‌lineage leading ​to Amaterasu ​and the ‌imperial ​house, while ‌the *Nihon ​Shoki* often ​presents ​variant traditions ​side by ‌side, preserving ‌conflicting ​genealogies and ‌episodes.

Because ​both texts ​were ‌compiled under ‌imperial patronage, ‌their portrayal ‌of ​Tsukuyomi is ‌never purely ​"mythological" in ​a ​neutral sense; ‌it is ​also a ​statement ​about legitimacy, ‌territory, and ​the proper ​ordering ​of the ‌human and ​divine worlds[^2]. ‌Modern ​readers must ‌therefore distinguish ​between the ‌older ‌narrative strata ​preserved in ​the chronicles ​and ​the ideological ‌framing imposed ‌by the ​compilers.

sections.label: Shinto Sources
sections.body:
Beyond ​the *Kojiki* ‌and ‌*Nihon ​Shoki*, the ​Shinto ​sources for ​**Tsukuyomi** ​include shrine ‌records ​(*engi*), ​ritual prayers ‌(*norito*), ​imperial ritual ‌protocols, ​and the ‌vast ​corpus ​of local ​festival ​traditions preserved ​at ‌shrines ​across Japan[^1]. ‌These ​documents reveal ‌how ​a figure ‌who ​begins ‌as a ​line ​in an ‌imperial ‌chronicle becomes ‌the ​focus ​of pilgrimage, ‌divination, ​and community ​identity. ‌The ​*Fudoki*, or ​provincial ‌gazetteers, add ​topographical ‌and etymological ​details ​that ​connect Tsukuyomi ​to ‌specific mountains, ‌rivers, ​and ‌villages.

Medieval ​and ​early-modern Shinto ‌texts ‌also reinterpret ‌Tsukuyomi ‌in ​light of ‌Buddhist, ​Confucian, and ​nativist ​agendas. The ‌early-modern ​*kokugaku* ​(National Learning) ​scholars, ‌in particular, ​sought ​to ​recover a ‌pure ​Shinto reading ‌of ​the figure, ‌stripped ​of ‌Buddhist accretions[^2]. ‌Their ​interpretations remain ​influential ​in contemporary ​shrine ‌theology ‌and popular ​understanding.

sources.citation: Ono, Sokyo, Shinto: The Kami Way (Tuttle, 1962).
Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

sections.label: Japanese Buddhist Sources
sections.body:
Japanese ​Buddhist ‌sources treat ‌**Tsukuyomi** ​through ​the lens ​of ​*honji-suijaku*, ​the theory ‌that ​local ​kami are ‌traces ​or ‌manifestations of ​universal ‌Buddhist ​truths. Medieval ​temple-shrine ​complexes ​produced rituals, ​images, ‌and ​narratives ‌that identified ​Tsukuyomi ‌with ​a Buddhist ‌counterpart, ​integrating ‌the figure ​into ​esoteric ‌mandalas, Pure ‌Land ‌devotion, ​and warrior ​protector ‌cults[^1]. ​These identifications ​were ‌not ​merely symbolic; ​they ‌reorganized ​the ‌ritual calendar, ​patronage ​networks, ​and sacred ​geography ‌of ‌the sites ​involved.

‌The ​Meiji-era policy ​of ‌*shinbutsu ‌bunri* formally ‌separated ‌kami ​and buddhas, ‌but ​Buddhist ​elements survived ​in ‌architecture, ​festival ​customs, and ​popular ‌iconography. ​Modern scholarship ​therefore ​reads ‌Tsukuyomi through ​both ‌Shinto ​and Buddhist ‌archives, ​recognizing ‌that the ‌two ​traditions ​shaped each ​other ​for ‌more than ‌a ​millennium[^2].

sources.citation: Teeuwen, Mark, and Fabio Rambelli, eds., Buddhas and Kami in Japan (Routledge, 2003).
Sonoda, Minoru, "Shinto and Buddhism," in Shinto in History, ed. Breen and Teeuwen (Curzon, 2000).
